title: Chapter 1 — Data Engineering Described: Quality Question Bank

questions.question: Which statement best matches the chapter's definition of data engineering?
options: Building systems and processes that take raw data and produce high-quality, consistent information for downstream use cases
Primarily building machine-learning models from structured datasets
Administering relational databases without responsibility for downstream use
Creating dashboards and KPIs for executive decision-making
questions.explanation: The chapter defines data engineering as developing, implementing, and maintaining systems/processes that turn raw data into high-quality, consistent information supporting uses such as analysis and ML.

questions.question: Which set is explicitly described as the intersection of data engineering?
options: ETL, dashboards, reporting, and data science
Networking, databases, statistics, and product management
BI, data science, machine learning, and cloud computing
Security, data management, DataOps, data architecture, orchestration, and software engineering
questions.explanation: These six disciplines are named in the chapter's definition.

questions.question: Where does the data engineering lifecycle begin and end according to the chapter?
options: At storage and at analytics
At source-system generation and at model training
With getting data from source systems and with serving data for use cases such as analysis or ML
With ingestion and with dashboard creation
questions.explanation: The lifecycle begins with getting data from source systems and ends with serving data for downstream use cases.

questions.question: Which sequence lists the chapter's five lifecycle stages in the correct order?
options: Ingestion → Generation → Storage → Transformation → Serving
Generation → Storage → Ingestion → Transformation → Serving
Storage → Generation → Transformation → Ingestion → Serving
Generation → Ingestion → Storage → Serving → Transformation
questions.explanation: The chapter lists Generation, Storage, Ingestion, Transformation, and Serving.

questions.question: What is the main conceptual purpose of the data engineering lifecycle?
options: To define the job hierarchy within a data organization
To replace the need for data architecture
To rank data tools by popularity
To shift attention from technology toward the data and the end goals it must serve
questions.explanation: The lifecycle is intended to prevent technology fixation and keep attention on data and business/use-case outcomes.

questions.question: Which group consists of lifecycle undercurrents rather than lifecycle stages?
options: Analytics, experimentation, ML
Generation, storage, ingestion
Transformation, serving, generation
Security, data management, DataOps, data architecture, orchestration, and software engineering
questions.explanation: Those six are the undercurrents that span the lifecycle.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT listed as something a data engineer typically does directly?
options: Understand how downstream consumers use data
Evaluate technology trade-offs
Build ML models directly
Build production-grade data systems
questions.explanation: The chapter says data engineers typically do not directly build ML models, reports/dashboards, analyses, KPIs, or software applications, although they should understand these areas.

questions.question: Why should a data engineer understand areas such as dashboards, KPIs, and ML even if they typically do not build them directly?
options: Because those areas replace data engineering
Because they are required lifecycle stages
Because understanding them helps the engineer serve stakeholders effectively
Because the chapter says every engineer must become a data scientist
questions.explanation: The chapter says engineers should have a good functioning understanding of these areas to serve stakeholders best.

questions.question: What historical development does the chapter identify as an important root of modern data engineering?
options: The rise of social media in the 2000s
The creation of Kubernetes
Data warehousing, with business data warehouses taking shape in the 1980s
The invention of deep learning in the 2010s
questions.explanation: The chapter traces roots to data warehousing, dating back to the 1970s, with business data warehousing taking shape in the 1980s.

questions.question: Who does the chapter credit with officially coining the term 'data warehouse' in 1989?
options: Bill Inmon
Ralph Kimball
Jeff Dean
Jesse Anderson
questions.explanation: The chapter says Bill Inmon officially coined the term in 1989.

questions.question: What role did Ralph Kimball and Bill Inmon play in the early data-warehouse era?
options: They created AWS and Hadoop
They invented MapReduce
They developed their respective data-modeling techniques and approaches
They defined Type A and Type B data engineers
questions.explanation: The chapter says Kimball and Inmon developed their respective eponymous data-modeling approaches.

questions.question: Why were BI engineer, ETL developer, and data warehouse engineer roles important historically?
options: They addressed needs created by data warehousing and were precursors to today's data engineering
They were primarily ML research roles
They replaced software engineers in web companies
They existed only after Hadoop
questions.explanation: The chapter describes these roles as precursors to today's data engineering and notes that they still play a central role.

questions.question: What pressure pushed companies such as Yahoo, Google, and Amazon beyond traditional monolithic relational systems in the early 2000s?
options: A requirement to use public cloud
The disappearance of data warehouses
A shortage of SQL developers
Traditional systems were being pushed to their limits by data growth
questions.explanation: The chapter says those companies initially relied on older systems but pushed them to their limits as data grew.

questions.question: Which qualities did the chapter say the next generation of systems needed as traditional systems buckled?
options: Encrypted, batch-only, monolithic, and licensed
Open source, serverless, graphical, and proprietary
Cost-effective, scalable, available, and reliable
Fast, cheap, relational, and centralized
questions.explanation: Those four qualities are explicitly listed.

questions.question: What combination of developments helped begin the 'big data' era?
options: The invention of dashboards
Cheap ubiquitous commodity hardware plus innovations in distributed computation and storage
The disappearance of web applications
Expensive proprietary hardware and centralized databases
questions.explanation: The chapter links cheap commodity hardware with distributed computation/storage innovations and the decentralization of monolithic services.

questions.question: What are the 'three Vs' commonly used in the chapter to describe big data?
options: Value, velocity, variety
Volume, validity, value
Verification, volume, velocity
Velocity, variety, volume
questions.explanation: The chapter names velocity, variety, and volume.

questions.question: Why are Google's 2003 Google File System paper and 2004 MapReduce paper called a 'big bang' for data engineering?
options: They directly created AWS
They formally created the data-engineer job title
They introduced the modern data stack
They provided cultural and technical roots that inspired later large-scale data technologies such as Hadoop
questions.explanation: The chapter acknowledges earlier antecedents but describes the Google papers as a major catalyst for data technologies and the cultural roots of modern data engineering.

questions.question: What was the significance of Yahoo's response to the Google papers?
options: Yahoo became the first public cloud
Yahoo created and later open sourced Apache Hadoop in 2006
Yahoo invented SQL
Yahoo launched Snowflake
questions.explanation: The chapter traces Hadoop to engineers at Yahoo inspired by the Google papers.

questions.question: Which set of technologies did Amazon create for its own exploding data needs and later expose through AWS?
options: BigQuery, Spanner, and Dataflow
Spark, Flink, and Beam
EC2, S3, and DynamoDB
HDFS, YARN, and Hive
questions.explanation: The chapter specifically names EC2, S3, DynamoDB, and other core building blocks.

questions.question: What was a defining characteristic of AWS's resource model in the chapter?
options: It required customers to maintain Hadoop clusters
It was limited to internal Amazon use
Customers had to buy and install physical hardware
It offered a pay-as-you-go marketplace for virtualized commodity hardware
questions.explanation: AWS is described as an ultra-flexible pay-as-you-go resource marketplace.

questions.question: What major processing shift occurred during the 2000s and 2010s?
options: From event streaming to batch
From cloud computing to physical data centers
From batch computing to event streaming
From relational databases to spreadsheets
questions.explanation: The chapter describes the transition from batch computing to event streaming as another major revolution.

questions.question: Why did the chapter say code-first engineering became fashionable during the big-data era?
options: Data warehouses stopped existing
GUI tools became mandatory
SQL disappeared permanently
MapReduce and related tools shifted work toward programming and low-level engineering
questions.explanation: The chapter says the ascendance of MapReduce helped make code-first engineering fashionable.

questions.question: What was a common misuse of big-data technology during its hype period?
options: Using Hadoop clusters for very small data problems
Using SQL for analytics
Using public clouds for large workloads
Using open source tools in enterprises
questions.explanation: The chapter gives the example of companies standing up Hadoop clusters to process only a few gigabytes.

questions.question: According to the chapter, what was the central reason the term 'big data' lost steam?
options: Data volumes decreased
Hadoop became illegal to use
Simplification made large-scale processing accessible without the same administrative burden
Companies stopped collecting data
questions.explanation: The chapter says, 'One word: simplification.' Managed and abstracted services reduced the overhead of operating big-data systems.

questions.question: What did big-data engineers often spend excessive time doing?
options: Delivering business insights
Maintaining complicated tooling and clusters
Building dashboards
Training AI researchers
questions.explanation: The chapter contrasts platform maintenance with delivering business insights and value.

questions.question: How does the chapter characterize the relationship between 'big data engineering' and today's data engineering?
options: Big-data engineering is now only an academic field
Big-data processing became accessible enough that big-data engineers are now simply data engineers
They are unrelated disciplines
Big data engineering replaced data engineering
questions.explanation: The chapter explicitly says big-data engineers are now simply data engineers.

questions.question: What trend characterizes data engineering in the 2020s according to the chapter?
options: A move toward decentralized, modularized, managed, highly abstracted tools
Elimination of third-party products
A return to monolithic, low-level frameworks
Less interoperability between systems
questions.explanation: The chapter describes a trend away from low-level monolithic frameworks toward managed, modular, abstracted tools.

questions.question: What does the chapter mean by describing data engineering as increasingly a discipline of 'interoperation'?
options: Data engineers build one giant platform
They avoid using third-party tools
They connect diverse technologies and sources to serve business goals
They focus only on interoperability testing
questions.explanation: The chapter compares connecting technologies to LEGO bricks in service of ultimate business goals.

questions.question: How does the chapter position data engineering relative to data science and analytics?
options: They are identical roles
Data science is upstream of data engineering
Data engineering is a subdiscipline of analytics
They are separate but complementary, with data engineering upstream of data science
questions.explanation: The authors explicitly argue that data engineering is distinct from data science and analytics and sits upstream of them.

questions.question: What does 'upstream' mean in the chapter's description of data engineering and data science?
options: Data engineers provide inputs that data scientists use to create useful outputs
Data engineers report to data scientists
Data scientists maintain source systems
Data engineers only work before software is written
questions.explanation: The chapter uses upstream/downstream to describe data engineers providing inputs to downstream data scientists.

questions.question: According to the chapter's discussion of Monica Rogati's hierarchy, where do data scientists spend an estimated 70–80% of their time?
options: Gathering, cleaning, and processing data
Executive presentations
Model deployment only
Analysis and ML
questions.explanation: The chapter says an estimated 70–80% is spent on the bottom three levels: gathering, cleaning, and processing data.

questions.question: What does the chapter say companies should do before tackling AI and ML?
options: Build a solid data foundation
Hire only AI researchers
Adopt the newest cloud technology
Eliminate data analysts
questions.explanation: The chapter says the bottom three levels of the hierarchy form a foundation that should be built before AI/ML.

questions.question: What should data engineers automate for data scientists when the engineering foundation is working well?
options: Model interpretation
The scientists' research agenda
All business decisions
Collecting, cleaning, and preparing data after initial exploratory work
questions.explanation: The chapter says data scientists should not have to spend their time on these tasks after initial exploration and data engineers should automate them as much as possible.

questions.question: What broader role does data engineering play between raw data and business value?
options: It eliminates the need for analytics
It replaces business leadership
It sits at the divide between getting data and getting value from data
It focuses only on data storage
questions.explanation: The chapter says data engineering straddles the divide between getting data and getting value from data.

questions.question: Which set of axes does the chapter say data engineers must constantly balance?
options: Accuracy, recall, precision, F1, and AUC
Latency, bandwidth, uptime, CPU, and RAM only
Cost, agility, scalability, simplicity, reuse, and interoperability
Revenue, hiring, marketing, sales, and growth
questions.explanation: Those six dimensions are explicitly listed as the balancing act of data engineering.

questions.question: How has the nature of data-engineering work changed as tools have become more abstract?
options: Engineers now maintain larger Hadoop clusters
Engineers spend more time on hardware installation
Engineers focus more on balancing simple, cost-effective best-of-breed services and agile architectures
Engineers no longer need software engineering skills
questions.explanation: The chapter says modern tooling reduces management complexity and shifts attention toward selecting services that deliver business value.

questions.question: What does the chapter say about coding for data engineers?
options: Data engineers should have production-grade software engineering chops
Coding is optional if the engineer knows SQL
Only ML engineers need production-grade coding skills
Managed services eliminate the need to code
questions.explanation: The chapter's short answer is yes: data engineers should have production-grade software engineering skills.

questions.question: What is the effect of managed services and plug-and-play SaaS on data-engineering work?
options: They force all pipelines into batch processing
They eliminate architecture decisions
They make software engineering irrelevant
They replace much low-level programming effort and encourage higher-level abstractions
questions.explanation: The chapter says fully managed services replace a great deal of low-level effort while engineers increasingly write pipelines as code within orchestration frameworks.

questions.question: Why does the chapter still value deep software-engineering and architectural knowledge in an abstracted world?
options: It is needed only for writing dashboards
It allows engineers to avoid managed services entirely
It replaces data architecture
It provides a competitive advantage when specific technical needs require deeper intervention
questions.explanation: The chapter says engineers who can dive into deep architectural details give their companies an edge when particular technical needs arise.

questions.question: What does the chapter mean by data maturity?
options: The amount of data stored
The age of a company's data platform
The number of data engineers employed
Progression toward higher data utilization, capabilities, and integration across the organization
questions.explanation: That is the chapter's definition, and it explicitly says maturity does not simply depend on age or revenue.

questions.question: Which statement best captures the chapter's point about company age/revenue and data maturity?
options: A young startup can be more data-mature than a large old company; what matters is how data is leveraged as competitive advantage
Revenue determines maturity
Only technology companies can reach high maturity
Older companies are always more mature
questions.explanation: The chapter explicitly contrasts an early-stage startup with a century-old billion-dollar company.

questions.question: Which situation most closely matches Stage 1, 'Starting with data'?
options: Formal data practices and specialized lifecycle teams
Custom data systems built around a mature competitive advantage
Fuzzy goals, early architecture, low adoption, a small team, and many ad hoc requests
Automated pipelines, self-service analytics, and seamless source onboarding
questions.explanation: Those characteristics define Stage 1 in the chapter.

questions.question: What is the primary goal of a data engineer in Stage 1?
options: Maximize cluster size
Create a large specialized data organization
Build advanced ML infrastructure first
Move fast, get traction, and add value
questions.explanation: The chapter states that a Stage 1 engineer's goal is to move fast, get traction, and add value.

questions.question: Why does the chapter caution against jumping headfirst into ML in Stage 1?
options: Stage 1 companies are prohibited from using ML
ML always costs more than data engineering
ML is never useful for startups
There may not be sufficient data or a scalable, repeatable means to deploy models
questions.explanation: Without a solid data foundation, reliable training data and scalable, repeatable production deployment are unlikely.

questions.question: Which is a recommended Stage 1 activity?
options: Deploy data catalogs enterprise-wide before defining goals
Build custom infrastructure regardless of available managed tools
Optimize cluster capacity as the primary objective
Get stakeholder buy-in and design architecture around business goals
questions.explanation: The Stage 1 recommendations include stakeholder buy-in and defining architecture around business goals.

questions.question: Why should quick wins in Stage 1/early Stage 2 be handled carefully?
options: Quick wins eliminate the need for stakeholder communication
Quick wins require abandoning architecture
Quick wins never create value
Quick wins can establish the importance of data but are likely to create technical debt
questions.explanation: The chapter says quick wins can build organizational support but likely create technical debt that should be reduced.

questions.question: What is the danger of a data team working in a silo during the early maturity stages?
options: The team may spend time building things that are of little use to people
The team will automatically overfit ML models
The team will hire too many analysts
The data warehouse will become relational
questions.explanation: The chapter emphasizes talking to stakeholders to avoid building low-value solutions.

questions.question: What is the chapter's rule for deciding when to build custom solutions?
options: Build custom solutions and code when doing so creates competitive advantage
Build custom systems whenever a Silicon Valley company does
Never write custom code
Always build custom systems for control
questions.explanation: The chapter repeatedly recommends off-the-shelf solutions for undifferentiated work and customization where it creates competitive advantage.

questions.question: What marks the transition into Stage 2, 'Scaling with data'?
options: The company moves away from ad hoc requests and establishes formal data practices
The company eliminates data architecture
The company returns to ad hoc requests
The company stops using data scientists
questions.explanation: Stage 2 is characterized by moving away from ad hoc data requests toward formal practices and scalable architectures.

questions.question: Which pair represents the stated goals for Stage 2?
options: Establish formal data practices and create scalable, robust data architectures
Focus exclusively on external-facing systems
Build AI research labs and eliminate technical debt completely
Replace all managed services and maximize custom code
questions.explanation: Those are the two explicit goals listed for Stage 2.

questions.question: What organizational change does the chapter associate with Stage 2?
options: All engineers become AI researchers
Data engineering roles generally move from generalists toward specialists
Data engineers stop collaborating with analysts
The data team becomes smaller by definition
questions.explanation: The chapter says roles move from generalists to specialists as the company formalizes and scales data practices.

questions.question: Which practice does the chapter recommend adopting in Stage 2?
options: Avoid all automation
Avoid stakeholder communication
Use only Hadoop
Adopt DevOps and DataOps practices
questions.explanation: Stage 2 goals include adopting DevOps and DataOps practices and building systems that support ML.

questions.question: According to the chapter, what is the main bottleneck for scaling data engineering?
options: The number of SQL queries
Storage capacity
Cluster nodes
The data engineering team
questions.explanation: The chapter explicitly says the main bottleneck is the data engineering team, not infrastructure resources.

questions.question: How should a Stage 2 organization respond to the temptation to adopt bleeding-edge tools used by famous companies?
options: Avoid all new technology
Adopt them immediately to stay competitive
Use only tools older than five years
Choose technology based on the value it will deliver to customers
questions.explanation: The chapter warns against social-proof-driven technology choices and says customer value should drive decisions.

questions.question: Which set best describes Stage 3, 'Leading with data'?
options: A data-driven organization with automated pipelines, self-service analytics/ML, seamless new-source introduction, and tangible value
Formal practices without automation
Ad hoc requests, low adoption, and a tiny generalist team
A company focused mainly on cluster administration
questions.explanation: These are defining characteristics of Stage 3.

questions.question: Which activity is specifically added to a Stage 3 data engineer's responsibilities?
options: Return to manual data requests
Create automation for seamless introduction and usage of new data
Stop collaborating with business teams
Avoid governance and quality work
questions.explanation: Stage 3 explicitly adds automation for seamless new-data introduction and usage.

questions.question: What 'enterprisey' aspects does Stage 3 emphasize?
options: Only dashboard design
Only server procurement
Only ML model tuning
Data management, including governance and quality, plus DataOps
questions.explanation: The chapter explicitly names data management, governance, quality, and DataOps.

questions.question: Which tools are specifically mentioned as ways to expose and disseminate data in Stage 3?
options: Firewalls, load balancers, and CDNs
Data catalogs, data lineage tools, and metadata management systems
Compilers, IDEs, and version-control servers
Spreadsheets, slide decks, and email
questions.explanation: Those three tool categories are explicitly listed.

questions.question: What is a major danger once an organization reaches Stage 3?
options: Using SQL effectively
Complacency and expensive technology hobby projects that fail to deliver business value
Automating new data sources
Having too much stakeholder communication
questions.explanation: The chapter warns that Stage 3 organizations must continuously maintain and improve and avoid expensive hobby projects.

questions.question: Why does the chapter say data engineering should be viewed through both business and technical lenses?
options: Because business responsibilities replace engineering responsibilities
Because technical skills are no longer important
Because the role exists only in business departments
Because engineers must understand both downstream requirements and technical systems/trade-offs
questions.explanation: The chapter describes data engineering as holistic, requiring understanding of data consumers and broader organizational implications alongside technical architecture.

questions.question: Which behavior is recommended for understanding an organization's human side?
options: Communicate only with engineers
Pay attention to hierarchies, reporting relationships, interactions, and silos
Ignore reporting lines and silos
Let technology determine organizational structure
questions.explanation: The chapter recommends observing organizational hierarchies, interactions, and silos to build trust and navigate the organization.

questions.question: What should a data engineer accomplish when scoping business and product requirements?
options: Choose a tool before understanding the problem
Avoid discussing requirements with stakeholders
Determine what to build and ensure stakeholders agree with the assessment
Optimize only for technical elegance
questions.explanation: The chapter says engineers need to know what to build and ensure stakeholder agreement, while understanding business impact.

questions.question: How does the chapter characterize Agile, DevOps, and DataOps?
options: Fundamentally cultural practices requiring organizational buy-in
Methods used only by project managers
Practices that eliminate the need for communication
Primarily tool categories
questions.explanation: The chapter explicitly says these practices are fundamentally cultural and require buy-in across the organization.

questions.question: Which three cost concepts does the chapter specifically say data engineers should optimize?
options: Hiring cost, office rent, and travel
Revenue, gross margin, and tax rate
CPU time, RAM, and disk space only
Time to value, total cost of ownership, and opportunity cost
questions.explanation: Those three are explicitly named under cost control.

questions.question: What does the chapter advise about continuous learning?
options: Chase every new tool
Focus on fundamentals while monitoring developments and filtering useful advances from immature ideas and fads
Ignore new developments
Specialize permanently in one framework
questions.explanation: The chapter recommends strong fundamentals plus awareness and filtering of new developments.

questions.question: What is the chapter's high-level technical architecture responsibility for a data engineer?
options: Always choose the most expensive tool
Optimize architectures for performance and cost using prepackaged or homegrown components
Build every component from scratch
Avoid architectural decisions
questions.explanation: The chapter says engineers must understand how to build architectures that optimize performance and cost using appropriate components.

questions.question: Which four are identified as the primary programming languages of data engineering 'at the time of this writing'?
options: Java, Scala, C#, and PowerShell
SQL, Python, a JVM language such as Java or Scala, and bash
SQL, Go, C++, and Julia
Python, R, JavaScript, and Rust
questions.explanation: The chapter explicitly lists SQL, Python, a JVM language, and bash.

questions.question: Why does the chapter describe Python as a bridge between data engineering and data science?
options: Python replaces SQL in databases
Many data-engineering tools are written in Python or expose Python APIs, and Python connects components
Python is the only language used by data scientists
Python is required by AWS
questions.explanation: The chapter calls Python a bridge because of its widespread role in data tools and APIs.

questions.question: Why are JVM languages such as Java and Scala useful to data engineers?
options: They replace bash on Linux
They are prevalent in Apache projects and can provide performance and lower-level access beyond Python APIs
They are the only languages used for dashboards
They are required for all SQL queries
questions.explanation: The chapter points to Spark, Hive, and Druid and notes JVM performance/lower-level access.

questions.question: What role does bash play in the chapter's list of primary languages?
options: It is mainly a database query language
It is a JVM language
It supports CLI scripting and OS operations, including pipeline and orchestration tasks
It is used to train ML models
questions.explanation: The chapter emphasizes bash/CLI productivity, scripting, OS operations, awk/sed, and orchestration calls.

questions.question: How did SQL's role change from the MapReduce era to the modern data landscape described in the chapter?
options: SQL disappeared entirely
SQL became useful only for small datasets
SQL was replaced by bash
SQL was briefly sidelined by custom MapReduce code but reemerged as the lingua franca of data
questions.explanation: The chapter explicitly describes SQL's reemergence after the MapReduce era.

questions.question: Which modern technologies are given as examples of systems that can process massive data using SQL semantics?
options: Only Hadoop HDFS
Only Python notebooks
Only Excel and spreadsheets
BigQuery, Snowflake, Spark SQL, and Hive
questions.explanation: The chapter lists Spark SQL, BigQuery, Snowflake, Hive, and others.

questions.question: Which statement best captures the chapter's position on SQL?
options: SQL is useful only for reporting
SQL should never be used for streaming
SQL is powerful and should be mastered, but engineers should recognize when another tool is more suitable
SQL is the only language a data engineer needs
questions.explanation: The chapter strongly advocates SQL proficiency while explicitly rejecting the idea that SQL is the be-all and end-all.

questions.question: Why might native Spark be preferable to SQL for some NLP preprocessing?
options: SQL is not declarative
A complex text-stemming/tokenization task can be more naturally and effectively implemented in native Spark than as an awkward SQL query
Spark is always cheaper
SQL cannot access data lakes
questions.explanation: The chapter uses text stemming/tokenization as an example of recognizing when SQL is not the right tool.

questions.question: Which of the following is listed as a secondary language that may be needed depending on company or domain tooling?
options: COBOL
Fortran
Go
Pascal
questions.explanation: The chapter lists R, JavaScript, Go, Rust, C/C++, C#, and Julia as possible secondary languages.

questions.question: What language is specifically noted as popular for user-defined functions in cloud data warehouses?
options: JavaScript
Bash
C#
Rust
questions.explanation: The chapter gives JavaScript as an example.

questions.question: What should engineers prioritize when keeping skills current?
options: Fundamentals that are unlikely to change, while monitoring developments and understanding how new technologies help the lifecycle
Avoiding all emerging technology
Only certifications
Only the newest tools
questions.explanation: That is the chapter's explicit advice for staying effective in a fast-moving field.

questions.question: What does 'A' stand for in Type A data engineer?
options: Analysis
Automation
Abstraction
Architecture
questions.explanation: Type A means abstraction: avoiding undifferentiated heavy lifting and unnecessary reinvention.

questions.question: What does 'B' stand for in Type B data engineer?
options: Benchmark
Build
Business
Batch
questions.explanation: Type B means build: creating custom data tools and systems where they provide competitive advantage.

questions.question: Which behavior best describes a Type A data engineer?
options: Build every platform internally
Avoid all vendor products
Use off-the-shelf products and managed services while keeping architecture abstract and straightforward
Focus exclusively on ML research
questions.explanation: Type A engineers avoid undifferentiated heavy lifting and mainly use off-the-shelf products, managed services, and tools.

questions.question: Which behavior best describes a Type B data engineer?
options: Use only SaaS products
Avoid custom engineering
Work only at Stage 1 companies
Build tools and systems that scale and leverage the company's core competency or competitive advantage
questions.explanation: That is the chapter's description of Type B.

questions.question: Where is a Type B data engineer more commonly found according to the chapter?
options: Only in academic institutions
More commonly in Stages 2 and 3, or in a unique mission-critical use case requiring custom tools
Only in companies with no data architecture
Only in Stage 1
questions.explanation: The chapter associates Type B more commonly with scaling/leading organizations or unique mission-critical use cases.

questions.question: Which statement about Type A and Type B engineers is explicitly supported?
options: A Type A engineer can never become Type B
They are mutually exclusive job titles
Type B is always more senior
They may work in the same company and can even be the same person
questions.explanation: The chapter says they may work together and may even be the same person; the distinction is about approach, not seniority.

questions.question: What is the central organizational position of the data engineer described in the chapter?
options: A replacement for business leadership
A purely downstream reporting role
A hub between data producers upstream and data consumers downstream
A role isolated from software engineering
questions.explanation: The chapter describes data engineers as a hub between producers such as software engineers/architects/DevOps and consumers such as analysts/data scientists/ML engineers.

questions.question: Which group is primarily upstream of data engineering in the chapter?
options: Executives and product managers only
Data analysts, data scientists, ML engineers
Data architects, software engineers, and DevOps/SREs
Customers and traders only
questions.explanation: These are the chapter's named upstream stakeholders.

questions.question: What do data architects primarily provide?
options: The blueprint for organizational data management, processes, architecture, and systems
Only ML infrastructure
Only dashboards
Only software application code
questions.explanation: The chapter describes architects as designing the blueprint and guiding data management, governance, and major initiatives.

questions.question: How has cloud computing affected the boundary between data architecture and data engineering?
options: It eliminated architecture
It made data engineers unable to do architecture
Cloud architectures are more fluid, so decisions that once required long lead times can often be made during implementation
It made on-premises architecture more fluid than cloud
questions.explanation: The chapter says cloud architecture decisions are often made during implementation rather than through long hardware/procurement cycles.

questions.question: Why must data engineers work closely with software engineers?
options: Software engineers replace analysts
Software engineers own all data governance
Software engineers generate application data and logs, and coordination is needed around volume, frequency, format, security, and compliance
They are both downstream consumers
questions.explanation: The chapter emphasizes collaboration from project inception and understanding the properties and constraints of source-system data.

questions.question: How are DevOps engineers and SREs characterized in relation to data engineering?
options: They replace data architects
They are never connected to data engineering
They may produce operational data and can be upstream or downstream depending on the work
They only build ML models
questions.explanation: The chapter classifies them as upstream through operational monitoring data while noting they may also consume data downstream or coordinate operations.

questions.question: What is the typical temporal focus of data scientists versus data analysts in the chapter?
options: Data scientists are forward-looking; analysts typically focus on past or present
Both focus only on real-time systems
Analysts focus only on ML
Data scientists focus on the past; analysts on the future
questions.explanation: That distinction is explicitly made.

questions.question: Which activity is characteristic of data analysts according to the chapter?
options: Running SQL queries in warehouses/lakes and using spreadsheets or BI tools to understand business performance and trends
Maintaining ML infrastructure
Designing cloud architectures
Training deep-learning models for production
questions.explanation: The chapter describes analysts as business/domain-focused users of SQL, spreadsheets, and BI tools.

questions.question: How do data analysts contribute to data engineering?
options: They only create software applications
They administer Hadoop clusters
They replace data engineers
Their subject-matter knowledge can help identify definitions, characteristics, and quality problems and improve data quality

questions.question: What is a primary responsibility of ML engineers?
options: Managing organizational data governance
Designing and maintaining infrastructure for ML processes at production scale, as well as developing/training advanced ML techniques
Replacing all data engineers
Creating executive dashboards only

questions.question: How does the chapter describe the boundaries among data engineering, data science, and ML engineering?

They are rigid and non-overlapping
They are identical roles
Only data engineers can work on ML systems

questions.question: What distinguishes an external-facing data engineer from an internal-facing one?

External-facing means working outside the company
External-facing work supports external applications and their feedback loops; internal-facing work primarily supports business and internal stakeholders
Internal-facing engineers never work with ML

Building an internal HR data mart
Maintaining a warehouse for executive dashboards
Building systems that collect application events and feed recommendations back into an ecommerce application

questions.question: Why can external-facing query systems require tighter query limits?
options: Because internal data is always larger
To eliminate security controls
To reduce the infrastructure impact of any single external user
Because external users cannot run SQL

External systems never have authentication
External queries may involve multitenant data containing many customers in a shared table
Internal systems are always public

questions.question: What relationship does the chapter describe between internal- and external-facing data engineering?
options: Internal-facing is obsolete
They are always completely separate
External-facing always comes first
They are often blended, and internal-facing data is usually a prerequisite for external-facing data

questions.question: What does the chapter say is the CEO's typical role regarding data and technology?

Managing every data pipeline
Defining a vision with technical C-suite roles and company data leadership rather than handling framework details
Writing production SQL

questions.question: What is the CIO primarily responsible for in the chapter?
options: External-facing application architecture
Data science research only
Internal-facing information technology, policies, and major IT initiatives
Product management

options: The CTO owns data governance exclusively
The CTO focuses only on internal ERP systems
The CTO is always below the CIO

Only project schedules

Only software deployment

Data governance only
Internal IT operations
Highly technical leadership focused specifically on data science and ML

options: They have identical responsibilities

Project managers write all pipelines

By replacing project management entirely
By managing only databases
By avoiding business stakeholders

Only an ML model
Any spreadsheet

Services/centralized and cross-functional models
Waterfall and Scrum
Type A and Type B

questions.question: What broad lesson does the chapter's conclusion give about being an engineer?
options: Engineers should understand the problems, tools, and people they work with and serve
Data engineers should avoid organizational concerns
Engineering is mainly isolated coding
